title: Thighplasty -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Thighplasty, or thigh lift surgery, is a body-contouring procedure that removes excess skin and subcutaneous tissue from the upper thighs, typically following massive weight loss, aging, or genetic skin laxity. The method improves contour, tightens the skin, and enhances the aesthetics of the lower body. Surgical techniques vary, ranging from limited crescent lifts to extensive vertical or spiral thighplasties, depending on the degree and distribution of skin redundancy. Preoperative assessment includes evaluation of skin quality, vascular status, and comorbidities that may impair wound healing. Complications can include wound dehiscence, seroma, infection, and lymphatic injury, emphasizing the importance of meticulous surgical planning and postoperative care.

title: Thighplasty -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Through participation in this educational activity, clinicians gain the knowledge and skills necessary to evaluate candidates for thighplasty, select appropriate surgical techniques, and manage perioperative risks to optimize patient outcomes. Participants enhance their understanding of anatomical considerations, wound closure strategies, and methods to prevent complications. Additionally, this course fosters interprofessional collaboration among surgeons, nurses, anesthesiologists, and rehabilitation specialists to promote patient-centered, safe, and effective care in body-contouring surgery.

title: Thighplasty -- Introduction
content: Thighplasty is a surgical procedure to remove excess lipodermal tissue from the medial thigh. Thighplasty aims to restore a normal anatomical appearance, improve the function of the upper thighs, and enhance overall quality of life. [1] As the incidence of bariatric surgeries in the United States has been rising over the last decade, the complications following surgeries to tackle excess skin after significant weight loss are becoming more prevalent. [2] [3] [4]

title: Thighplasty -- Introduction
content: Despite previously being considered solely a cosmetic procedure, the indications for thighplasty have evolved to improve functionality in amputees and promote increased mobility, improved hygiene, and better treatment outcomes for recurrent cutaneous irritation and infections in patients who are obese or have undergone massive weight loss. [5] Thighplasty techniques have also evolved and improved to minimize morbidity and achieve more desirable cosmetic outcomes. [6] [7] [8] While medial thighplasty to resect tissue in the groin and along the medial compartment of the lower extremity results in less visible scarring, incisional healing can be compromised by postoperative infections or frictional trauma. Thighplasty requires precision, and over- or under-resecting tissue must be avoided to minimize complications and maximize thigh symmetry and cosmesis. This activity reviews the clinically relevant anatomy, indications, contraindications, complications, best technical practices, and care for patients undergoing thighplasty.

title: Thighplasty -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Thighplasty was initially introduced in the 1950s and was not widely accepted for many years due to high complication rates. The initially described thighplasty technique resulted in scar migration, leading to vulvar deformities due to a poor understanding of the thigh's anatomy. [9] [10] As this understanding has evolved, knowledge of the thigh's anatomy has become crucial for maximizing cosmetic outcomes while minimizing patient morbidity.

title: Thighplasty -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: In both phenotypic sexes, the medial thigh is associated with a skin-fat envelope less tightly adherent to the underlying fascia; the dermal component is especially thin. [11] This anatomy makes the medial thigh compartment more prone to redundancy and laxity, leading to skin ptosis that can extend to the knee in severe cases. This anatomy is also why medial thighplasty has gained favor over a lateral or posterior approach.

title: Thighplasty -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The femoral triangle, located adjacent to the intertriginous fold of the inguinal crease, is an important anatomical landmark denoting the transition from the pelvis to the leg. The femoral artery, vein, nerve, and sheath pass through the femoral triangle, with the femoral sheath acting as a potential space for displaced abdominal contents and a resulting femoral hernia. A significant disruption of the lymphatics in this region can increase the incidence of complications after thighplasty. During thighplasty, it is important to maintain a superficial approach, as the procedure focuses on removing excess lipodermal tissue without affecting the crucial underlying structures. [12]

title: Thighplasty -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: The great saphenous vein and its branches are found in the medial thigh tissue; this vein ascends along the medial aspect of the thigh and confluences with the femoral vein at the saphenofemoral junction just caudal to the femoral triangle. [9] Intraoperative preservation of the great saphenous vein is crucial to reduce the risk of postoperative venous insufficiency. However, there are reports of concurrent saphenous vein stripping or ligation during thighplasty performed on patients with preoperative venous insufficiency and ultrasonographic evidence of saphenous reflux.

title: Thighplasty -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Other critical anatomical structures to consider during thighplasty include the superficial lymphatics. These lymphatics are concentrated in the medial thigh, converge at the femoral triangle, and run deep to the great saphenous vein. [11] Significant damage to the superficial lymphatics can lead to severe sequelae, such as lymphocele or postoperative lymphedema. Maintaining a relatively superficial dissection during thighplasty has resulted in successful outcomes while reducing lymphatic-associated morbidity. [13]

title: Thighplasty -- Anatomy and Physiology
content: Historically, thighplasty was associated with high rates of untoward scar migration. Lockwood introduced a method anchoring the inferior flap in a transverse incision, or the anterior flap in a vertical incision, to the peritoneal membranous superficial fascia, otherwise known as the deep membranous layer of the superficial fascia or the Colles fascia. [10] [14] This fascial layer is contiguous with the Scarpa fascia anteriorly and attaches to the ischiopubic ramus proximally and fascia lata distally. Originally thought of as a durable aponeurotic plane suitable for anchoring tissue, recent studies have demonstrated that variability in the composition of the Colles fascia leads to inconsistent long-term outcomes and associated morbidity. [15]

title: Thighplasty -- Indications
content: The incidence of thighplasties over the last decade has increased alongside that of bariatric surgery. Thighplasties were initially considered solely cosmetic procedures, usually performed after substantial weight loss. In this group of patients who have significant weight loss, the severity and distribution of lipodystrophy, redundancy, or ptotic skin of the thighs can lead to multiple functional complaints. These include skin irritation or infection, reduced mobility, pain and discomfort, and difficulty in finding correctly fitting clothes. Here, thighplasties not only serve to improve cosmesis but also to improve function.

title: Thighplasty -- Indications
content: The Pittsburgh Rating Scale (PRS) is a validated rating system to classify skin contour deformities following massive weight loss. [16] The PRS evaluates 10 anatomical regions using a 4-point grading scale ranging from 0 (normal) to 3 (severe). The PRS may be used as a preoperative tool to assist in planning and anticipating surgical outcomes for thighplasty. Less severe skin contour deformities may benefit from minimally invasive procedures such as liposuction. In contrast, those with a more severe deformity require extensive procedures such as excision, considerable undermining, and tissue repositioning. Thighplasty has improved mobility and functionality in patients after lower extremity amputation by improving prosthesis fit. [5] Thighplasty is an affordable and practical solution for patients with obesity who have undergone transfemoral amputation when compared with repeated iterations of sockets to mold an amputation stump.

title: Thighplasty -- Indications
content: Wounds caused by genitoperineal defects caused by infection, trauma, or neoplasm have led to increased versatility of thighplasty with the expectation of closing a gruesome wound with an excellent cosmetic and functional outcome. [17] For example, hidradenitis suppurativa is a chronic inflammatory disease frequently involving the moist skin creases of the axillae and groin. Medically refractory cases of hidradenitis suppurativa complicated by recurrent abscesses may require radical excision, often combining thighplasty with regional or free tissue transfer to augment the tissue loss and allow for healing by primary intention. [18] Thighplasty has a wide breadth of indications and is an adaptable procedure with the foundational purpose of restoring appearance and functionality.

title: Thighplasty -- Contraindications
content: While there are no absolute contraindications to thighplasty, modifiable and nonmodifiable relative contraindications exist. Patients with comorbidities such as diabetes mellitus, cardiovascular disease, renal insufficiency, anemia, and pulmonary disease should be medically optimized in the preoperative period to improve surgical outcomes and to reduce the risk of complications (both anesthetic and surgical). If patients have multiple poorly managed comorbidities, the surgeon should assess whether they are fit for surgery and, if not, the procedure should not be considered. A thorough preoperative evaluation to assess for peripheral vascular or lymphatic disease can help achieve a favorable outcome and mitigate complications.

title: Thighplasty -- Contraindications
content: Lymphedema is an incurable, chronic, debilitating diagnosis; management is focused on limiting secondary complications. [19] The symptoms of lymphedema include aching, heaviness, pitting edema, and recurrent infections in the affected limb. Lymphedema can easily be confused with excess lipodermal tissue, and patients may warrant further investigation with lymphoscintigraphy if the diagnosis is uncertain. Further disruption of lymphatic channels in a patient with already poor lymphatic drainage may accelerate the disease process and its associated complications. Before performing a thighplasty, it is essential to conduct a thorough evaluation to assess for lymphedema.

title: Thighplasty -- Contraindications
content: The prevalence of chronic venous insufficiency in patients with obesity is increasing; a thighplasty could lead to superficial venous disruption and progression of venous insufficiency. [20] Additionally, any history of venous thromboembolism should be considered in the preoperative assessment. Patients electing to undergo thighplasty will benefit from maintaining a stable preoperative weight. While no data cite an ideal timeframe for weight stability, many practitioners advocate delaying thighplasty until the patient has demonstrated a stable weight for 1 year. [21] Preoperative weight stability helps to define the extent of lipodystrophy and optimizes tissue resection.

title: Thighplasty -- Contraindications
content: In addition to well-recognized comorbidities, smoking and poorly controlled diabetes are among the strongest predictors of postoperative complications in thighplasty, particularly wound dehiscence and infection. Active smoking is associated with impaired perfusion, delayed healing, and higher rates of flap necrosis, and most guidelines recommend a minimum of 4 to 6 weeks of smoking cessation before elective surgery. Patients with untreated psychiatric conditions, especially body dysmorphic disorder, should also be approached with caution, as postoperative dissatisfaction may be high regardless of technical outcome. A structured psychosocial assessment tool has been proposed to help screen high-risk patients. [22] These considerations highlight the importance of a comprehensive, multidisciplinary preoperative evaluation beyond traditional medical optimization.

title: Thighplasty -- Contraindications
content: Expectations regarding the outcome of thighplasty need to be clearly defined, reasonable, and mutually agreed upon. If the surgeon and the patient cannot agree on the expected result, there must be a genuine consideration of the appropriateness of the procedure. The prevalence of body dysmorphic disorder in aesthetic plastic surgery practices has been reported to be up to 40%, and a high index of suspicion is warranted. [23]

content: The equipment needed for thighplasty includes the following: Sterile marking pen Liposuction system with or without ultrasound Monopolar and bipolar electrocautery Basic plastic surgery instrument tray Absorbable and nonabsorbable suture Dressing supplies, including Xeroform gauze Compression leggings

title: Thighplasty -- Preparation
content: The preoperative evaluation is essential to a thighplasty and must include a discussion of the surgical technique, possible complications, and expected outcomes. A thorough assessment of the location of skin ptosis, subcutaneous fat distribution, and skin quality, laxity, and thickness must accompany a comprehensive physical examination to assess for signs of peripheral arterial disease, venous insufficiency, lymphedema, and other comorbidities. The medical history and physical examination will inform the choice of surgical technique.

title: Thighplasty -- Preparation
content: Surgeon-led marking in the preoperative holding area supports surgical planning and is crucial to the procedure's outcome. [24] The patient should be marked while standing upright with legs abducted and in recumbent body and limb positions; this allows complete visualization of the extent of the excess tissue. Importance should be placed on the lipodermal tissue laxity and anticipated scar location, as well as the traction that will be placed on the horizontal incision and its proximity to the labia majora or scrotum to reduce any potential distortion.

title: Thighplasty -- Preparation
content: Thighplasty is performed under general anesthesia with the patient in the lithotomy position. Lithotomy positioning distorts tissue orientation; preoperative identification and marking of the tissue to be resected are imperative. Postoperatively, sequential compression devices are applied, and pharmacological venous thromboembolism prophylaxis is initiated to reduce the risk of deep venous thrombosis. [2]

title: Thighplasty -- Technique or Treatment
content: There have been several advances in the thighplasty technique since it was first described in the 1950s. Currently, the most common approach is to the medial thigh, as this is where skin laxity and ptosis are most prominent, and there are multiple approaches to medial thighplasty. The methods commonly used to address lipodystrophy and excess lipodermal tissue in the thigh include isolated liposuction, a horizontal or transverse lift, a vertical lift, a combined lift, which can be further differentiated into the T-shaped or L-shaped lift, and a double triangle. All of these procedures can be performed with or without concomitant liposuction. [25] The preoperative evaluation will guide the choice of the appropriate technique depending on individual patient needs. Isolated liposuction is reserved for patients with a low PRS score or isolated excess subcutaneous tissue; the lack of skin ptosis makes thighplasty an unfavorable approach in these individuals. Liposuction is tolerated with good results in appropriately selected patients. [26] Unfortunately, isolated liposuction does not address the excess skin in patients with ptotic skin and may exacerbate symptoms and increase complications.

title: Thighplasty -- Technique or Treatment
content: A horizontal thighplasty utilizes an incision created in the intertriginous folds of the groin, approximately 1 cm caudal to the inguinal crease, extending from the femoral triangle to the middle of the infrabuttock crease. [11] This technique is employed to lift the tissue cephalad, most commonly to address skin ptosis over the proximal thigh. An essential step in this technique is anchoring the inferior flap to the Colles fascia to limit caudal migration of the resulting scar. [24] The vertical thighplasty, performed to reduce circumferential skin laxity in patients with excess lipodermal tissue extending to the knee level, creates an incision along the medial thigh to hide the scar when viewed from the front. An elliptical incision is planned along the medial part of the thigh, extending from 3 cm caudal to the labia majora or scrotum to slightly above the medial condyle of the knee. [11] The width of the incision is determined using the "pinch test" to estimate the amount of redundant skin to excise. The cephalad portion of the incision is typically extended along the infrabuttock crease to address resulting tissue redundancy.

title: Thighplasty -- Technique or Treatment
content: A combined horizontal and vertical approach is frequently the best technique for patients with abundant lipodermal tissue involving the entire thigh who require circumferential tissue reduction in addition to elevation. A T-shaped lift has a vertical incision extending from the middle of the transverse incision and running down the medial thigh. The L-shaped lift, a slight variation, has the vertical incision originating from the posterior aspect of the horizontal incision. The planned vertical incision has a gentle curve, coursing back down the middle of the thigh for preferred scar placement. The resultant scar forms an inverted "T" or "L." The double triangle thighplasty addresses excess tissue in the mons region and the medial thigh. [27]

title: Thighplasty -- Technique or Treatment
content: When considering adjunctive liposuction, there is no consensus on whether this should be accomplished as a staged or simultaneous approach. However, using liposuction to thin the skin envelope and reduce fat deposits has improved incisional planning and estimations of skin resection and scar location, resulting in more desirable outcomes in some series. [24] [9] If liposuction is pursued simultaneously, the superficial subcutaneous layers of the medial and anterior thigh compartments are infiltrated with a tumescent solution, and liposuction is performed. Repeat evaluation of excess skin and planned incisions should be performed, as it is typical for extra skin removal to be required after liposuction. [28] Any additional modifications should be made from the anterior line, as the anterior thigh compartment is more mobile than the posterior. [29]

Repeat evaluation of excess skin and planned incisions should be performed, as it is typical for extra skin removal to be required after liposuction. [28] Any additional modifications should be made from the anterior line, as the anterior thigh compartment is more mobile than the posterior. [29]

title: Thighplasty -- Technique or Treatment
content: In all techniques, it is crucial to remain superficial to the fascia lata to limit disruption of the superficial lymphatic system and vessels coursing along the medial thigh. [25] Using penetrating towel clamps or permanent sutures can help approximate skin edges before wound closure to ensure the wound closes with acceptable tension and produces an optimal scar. Recent refinements in thighplasty emphasize tension-reducing strategies and lymphatic preservation. Techniques such as liposuction-assisted medial thighplasty reduce flap thickness and limit undermining, thereby lowering seroma and wound complication rates compared to excision alone.

title: Thighplasty -- Technique or Treatment
content: Energy-based devices (radiofrequency, plasma, laser) are increasingly explored as adjuncts for skin tightening in mild to moderate laxity, with early reports suggesting shorter recovery and reduced scar burden. For patients with massive weight loss and extensive ptosis, combined vertical and horizontal approaches remain the standard. Still, the use of progressive-tension sutures and fascial anchoring has reduced scar migration rates. These innovations continue to shift thighplasty from a purely resectional procedure to a hybrid contouring operation tailored to functional and cosmetic needs. [8]

title: Thighplasty -- Complications
content: Unfortunately, thighplasty is a procedure associated with high morbidity, with recent studies' results citing around a 42% complication rate. [25] The complication rate for thighplasty remains relatively high despite evolving surgical techniques aimed at mitigating associated complications. Patients must be informed of these potential complications before undergoing thighplasty. Despite relatively high overall complication rates, severe and life-threatening complications are extremely rare. VTEs are the most serious complication following thighplasty, while rates for developing a VTE (including deep vein thrombosis or pulmonary embolism) are low, documented as 1% in current literature. [30]

title: Thighplasty -- Complications
content: The complications of thighplasty range from simple and easily handled, such as an asymptomatic seroma, to severe and debilitating, such as vulvar displacement or lymphedema. Due to the scar's anatomical location, its proximity to the genital and perianal areas, and the prevalence of sweat glands in the groin, the wound is highly susceptible to infection in the postoperative period. [9] Wound-specific complications include, but are not limited to, dehiscence (51%), infection (16%), and necrosis (5%). [30] Other common complications include seroma (25%), hematoma (6%), lymphocele, scar migration, hypertrophic scarring, and vulvar widening. [30] [31] [32] Debilitating complications include thrombophlebitis and lymphedema. Complications, including scar migration, hypertrophy, or asymmetry, are most likely to require reoperation.

title: Thighplasty -- Complications
content: Study results have cited higher complication rates in patients with higher preoperative body mass index, undergoing more technically advanced or concomitant procedures, and those with more underlying comorbidities, specifically diabetes mellitus and tobacco use. [25] [32] Although not a technical complication, patient dissatisfaction is a potentially severe and relatively common outcome. [33] Establishing a shared understanding of realistic expectations is fundamental to successful outcomes following thighplasty.

title: Thighplasty -- Complications
content: Beyond immediate wound-related morbidity, long-term complications deserve emphasis. Chronic lymphedema may persist in up to 5% of cases, leading to recurrent infections and diminished quality of life. Neuropraxia of the medial femoral cutaneous nerve can cause sensory loss or neuropathic pain, which may require prolonged management. Significantly, recent series show that liposuction-assisted thighplasty reduces overall complication rates by nearly half, particularly infection and seroma. Stratifying patients by body mass index, smoking status, and comorbidities allows for better risk counseling and has been shown to reduce reoperation rates in high-volume centers. [34]

title: Thighplasty -- Clinical Significance
content: The increased prevalence of significant weight loss, whether through bariatric surgery or newly emerging weight-loss medications such as glucagonlike peptide-1 (GLP-1) receptor agonists (eg, semaglutide, tirzepatide), is increasing demand for body-contouring procedures, including thighplasty. Thighplasty has evolved and adapted to improve technical efficiency and patient outcomes while mitigating associated complications. [35] Associated complications are often outweighed by an enhanced quality of life resulting from improving cosmesis, functionality, and mobility related to redundant and ptotic skin in appropriately selected patients. [36] Indications for thighplasty have expanded beyond cosmetic benefits to include the repair of traumatic wounds, the excision of genitoperineal disease, and improved prosthesis fit. [5] [17]

title: Thighplasty -- Clinical Significance
content: With the advent of GLP-1 receptor agonists, a new population of patients with rapid, medically induced weight loss is emerging, increasing the demand for body contouring procedures. This differs from postbariatric individuals, as weight loss is often faster, and patients may present with different distributions of skin laxity and unique nutritional considerations. Thighplasty thus represents a bridge between functional rehabilitation and aesthetic improvement, addressing friction, hygiene, mobility, and body image. Quality-of-life studies consistently show high patient satisfaction despite elevated complication rates, underscoring its clinical value when performed in appropriately selected candidates. [37]

title: Thighplasty -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Thighplasty is a complex procedure that requires an interprofessional, team-based approach for optimal patient outcomes. [17] [38] Successful results depend on comprehensive coordination among surgeons, advanced practitioners, nurses, pharmacists, nutritionists, physical therapists, and other specialists. Physicians and advanced practitioners must have expertise in surgical techniques, anatomic variations, and perioperative management to minimize complications such as seroma, wound dehiscence, or infection. Preoperative planning begins with a detailed assessment by the plastic surgeon, incorporating patient factors such as comorbidities, nutritional status, and personal goals. Patients may also benefit from consultation with vascular surgeons, internists, bariatric surgeons, or mental health professionals to address underlying medical or psychosocial issues that could influence outcomes.

title: Thighplasty -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: During the perioperative phase, nurses play a critical role in wound management, drain care, patient education, and pain management, acting as advocates and key communicators between patients and surgeons. [11] Pharmacists contribute by ensuring appropriate antibiotic prophylaxis, evaluating drug interactions, and developing multimodal pain regimens to minimize opioid use and prevent complications such as venous thromboembolism. [2] Nutritionists are essential in optimizing preoperative nutritional status, particularly in postbariatric patients, by implementing dietary plans that promote adequate protein intake and prevent postoperative weight gain. Physical therapists facilitate safe mobility and rehabilitation postoperatively, promoting early movement and functional recovery. This collaborative, multidisciplinary strategy enhances patient-centered care, reduces complication rates, and improves overall satisfaction and safety. Through coordinated communication, shared decision-making, and role-specific expertise, the healthcare team can ensure that patients undergoing thighplasty receive the highest-quality care, leading to improved functional and aesthetic outcomes.
